purpose: Phenelzine is used to treat depression, especially when other antidepressants have not worked well. It can also help with anxiety and phobias. Doctors may prescribe it when someone has not responded to more commonly used antidepressants.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers like serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine to regulate your mood. An enzyme called monoamine oxidase breaks these chemicals down too quickly in some people with depression. Phenelzine blocks that enzyme, allowing more of these mood-boosting chemicals to stay active in your brain longer.
common_side_effects: Dizziness when standing up too quickly, drowsiness, dry mouth, trouble sleeping, weight gain, swelling in the feet or ankles, constipation, and sexual problems are among the most common side effects people notice.
warnings: This medication has very serious food and drug interactions. You must strictly avoid foods high in tyramine — such as aged cheeses, cured meats, red wine, soy sauce, and certain beers — because combining them with phenelzine can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure called a hypertensive crisis. You also cannot take many other medications with it, including most other antidepressants, cold medicines, or pain relievers like tramadol, without risking a life-threatening reaction. Always carry a list of medications you take and check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking anything new, including over-the-counter products.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 15 mg taken three times a day. Your doctor may slowly increase this to find the dose that works best for you, sometimes up to 60 to 90 mg per day in divided doses. Once you feel better and your condition is stable, your doctor may gradually lower your dose to the smallest effective amount.
